pix/host/supervise._prod_loc_note: Then the daemon runtime: a third [[services]] runtime for a long-running HOST process that already speaks its own protocol on a loopback port. It exists because go-plugin is the wrong shape for one -- snow-proxy is reached over HTTP by an in-sandbox wrapper, so a net/rpc handshake would replace a working transport to gain nothing -- and because the Port/Listen/Health fields on Service were designed for exactly this and had no runtime that read them. It reuses everything that matters (staged copy-then-verify, env allowlist, restart budgets, the permanent-vs-transient split, and the rule that a running process is not health) and adds only launch + probe. The doctor row is the point: a pack daemon was the one host-exec facet with NO row, so when snow-proxy died the warehouse capability degraded in total silence. Then the third launch form. UnitSpec described only two ways to start a unit -- self-exec or a SHA-pinned external path -- so Validate rejected the one thing a pack daemon actually is: a binary the user built on their own Mac, which no shared manifest can carry a SHA for. The pack was accepted, the tree accepted the daemon, and then the unit it was handed could not describe itself, so snow-proxy never started and the failure surfaced only in a serve log. UnitSpec.Command closes that, joins identity() so a reattach cannot confuse two daemons, and is refused alongside a sha pin -- a pin naming a file the spec never reads is worse than no pin, because it reads as a guarantee. The consent screen renders it UNPINNED so the absence is the user's call, not a silent property. And the startup budget. waitHealthy took HealthTimeout, the per-probe budget, for a daemon's FIRST health check -- so snow-proxy (~1.5s warm, ~3.5s cold) lost a coin flip against 3s, and a lost flip removes the unit from the tree, which a first-run user meets as a dead warehouse. Handshake already meant exactly 'how long may a unit take to become usable', so it now covers both unit kinds rather than growing a fourth timeout, and AddDaemon's outer wait derives from the same budget instead of firing while the inner poll is still legitimately running. The added lines are that comment plus countTrue; the launch path itself did not grow. Then hostpath.go, prod_loc 1703 -> 1815 and globals 29 -> 30 (errCommandNotFound). 'Resolved on PATH at launch' meant nothing in the environment that actually launches serve: launchd hands a login service PATH=/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin, and every host binary in this system lives elsewhere -- snow-proxy and slack-mcp in ~/.local/bin, snow and gog and op under Homebrew. So the daemon resolved perfectly in a developer's shell and failed PERMANENTLY under the managed service, which is the only way real users run it, while the error said 'is not on PATH' to someone whose interactive PATH did have it. The same gap hit the child: a daemon inheriting launchd's PATH starts, binds, and answers its health check while being unable to find the vendor CLI it shells out to -- every row green, capability broken, which is the defect class this whole release was about. Resolution now searches PATH then three code-pinned directories, the error names every one of them, and a unit that allowed PATH gets the same list so it can find its own tools. The list is pinned in code, not config: a manifest that could extend it could point `command` anywhere while keeping the same name on the consent screen. Then 1815 -> 1825: a daemon never recorded its probe latency, so `pix serve status` printed probe=0us for an HTTP GET over a socket. Zero reads as 'instant', not as 'never measured', and the latency of the probe that timed out is the number that explains the eviction after it -- which is why the go-plugin unit has always timed every probe, failures included. Now both kinds do. Then 1825 -> 1919: a port probe cannot tell 'my child is serving' from 'someone else owns this port', and that gap ran snow-proxy 4,057 times over six hours on Mark's Mac. An orphan held :11442 (pkill of a foreground serve leaves the daemon behind, because Setpgid puts it in its own group), so every generation was: child starts, cannot bind, exits 1, while waitHealthy dialled the port, got the ORPHAN's 200 and reported healthy. `pix doctor` said `daemons OK 1 answering` throughout, because something genuinely was. The fix is a PRE-FLIGHT dial before launching: nothing of ours is running yet, so anything listening is someone else's and the bind is guaranteed to fail. It is deterministic where catching it afterwards is a race, because a child that exits in microseconds may not be reaped before the probe returns -- which is why the obvious after-the-fact check failed its own test first. It waits up to the stop budget before concluding, so a restart that is moments from releasing its own socket is not condemned. waitHealthy also watches the child now and refuses to believe a passing probe once it has exited, which covers the non-port causes. Then prod_loc 1919 -> 1971: tryReattach REAPS the live child it refuses to adopt. Refusing was already right; walking away was the bug. When the persisted state names this unit and a pid proven alive and ours, but the identity fingerprint or the negotiated protocol version no longer matches, that pid is our OWN earlier generation -- the ordinary upgrade (pix-host rebuilt or upgraded while a hard-killed supervisor's child kept running). The old code dropped the record and left the process running: unsupervised, now unfindable, still holding memory's exclusive store flock, so every later spawn died on the lock and `serve` could not start again at all. Observed on a real host on 2026-08-23 (`supervise: memory reattach_rejected executable identity changed`, then a launchd KeepAlive respawn loop every 10s against a plugin orphaned since Aug 15), and reproduced both ways against the real binary before and after. The switch reorders so liveness/address precede the two supersede cases, which is what makes their kill decision sound; the kill itself is unchanged policy, factored into reapVerifiedOrphan -- now killVerifiedOrphan's ONLY caller, so both the dispense-failure path and the new supersede path reach an OS process through exactly one set of proofs (revalidateOrphan, start-time-bound against pid reuse). stopChild stops revoking the reattach record when its kill missed the stop budget and the child is not confirmed exited: that was the same orphan-with-no-record leak by a second route. Three `pid <= 0` guards (killVerifiedOrphan, revalidateOrphan, processAlive) are unreachable today but sit on primitives where a non-positive pid means the process GROUP -- the difference between reaping an orphan and killing the supervisor and everything it started. Comments were compressed hard first (+80 -> +52); no new exports or globals. A deliberate, reviewed raise of a shrink-only budget.

pix/host/sys._prod_loc_note: prod_loc 489 -> 536, globals 12 -> 14: the cross-process flock is BOUNDED. It was a plain blocking LOCK_EX, and a blocking wait with no deadline is a hang with no diagnosis — `pix pack use` registered every server and then went silent, waiting inside its post-commit wrapper refresh for a lock another process held. A post-commit side effect is exactly the code that is allowed to fail with a note rather than take the terminal with it, and it could not: the caller can report a timeout, it cannot report a wait that never ends. acquireFlock polls LOCK_NB to a deadline (blocking on a goroutine plus a select would leak that goroutine, still holding the fd, for as long as the holder lives) and the error names the lock file so `lsof` finds the holder. Ordinary contention still acquires. A deliberate, reviewed raise of a shrink-only budget. Then 536 -> 554, globals 14 -> 16: the wait SAYS SO. Bounding it fixed the hang and left the symptom that made the hang hard to read — a blank terminal, indistinguishable from a wedged one. A real `pix setup` sat silent for ten seconds while working perfectly, and there was no way to tell that from the outside. Past a second of waiting, acquireFlock names the lock on stderr, once; an uncontended lock stays silent, which is the second test. A deliberate, reviewed raise of a shrink-only budget.
